nameStory: The Spotted Cobweaver gets its name from the distinctive markings on its abdomen and its web-building style. Like other comb-footed spiders, it creates irregular, messy webs that look more like cobwebs than the perfect orb webs we often picture spiders making.
description: The Spotted Cobweaver is a small, delicate spider that belongs to the comb-footed spider family. These spiders are relatively tiny, typically measuring just a few millimeters in body length. They have the characteristic round abdomen of their family, often marked with subtle spots or patterns that give them their common name. Their legs are long and thin relative to their body size, and they move with quick, jerky motions when disturbed.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates irregular, three-dimensional cobwebs that feel sticky and tangled when accidentally walked into, quite different from organized orb webs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, delicate build with a rounded abdomen and thin legs that feel almost thread-like if you gently brush against the web

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for subtle spotting or mottled patterns on the abdomen, though these may be faint and require close observation

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, with the body typically no larger than a small peppercorn, easy to overlook

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in its web and quickly retreats to web corners when disturbed, often dropping on a silk line

habitat: Found in sheltered outdoor locations like under eaves, in garden sheds, or among dense vegetation where they can anchor their irregular webs. They prefer spots that are protected from direct rain and wind but still allow access to flying insects. Look for them in corners of structures, between fence posts, or in thick shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Adult spiders become active and begin building webs in protected locations. This is when you're most likely to walk into fresh webs stretched across pathways.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults actively hunting and mating. Webs are most noticeable and well-developed during warm, humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Females create egg sacs and adults begin seeking winter shelter. Webs may appear more abundant as spiders move to find protected overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with eggs overwintering in protected silk sacs. Webs may persist as empty, dusty remnants until spring.

funFact: Despite being so tiny you could easily mistake one for a speck of dirt, Spotted Cobweavers are actually related to the infamous Black Widow spider and share the same family trait of having a 'comb' of bristles on their back legs that they use like tiny fingers to wrap up prey!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small comb-footed spiders or even dismissed as 'just a tiny spider.' The irregular, messy web is your best clue - if it's not a neat orb web or funnel web, but rather looks like the classic 'cobweb' in a horror movie, you're likely looking at a comb-footed spider.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'cobweb' actually comes from the old English word 'coppe,' meaning spider, so cobweavers are literally 'spider-web weavers.' Many people think all spider webs are the same, but cobweavers create the irregular, dusty webs we associate with abandoned buildings.
compareHints: Since this is the only Thymoites species in our region, compare it with other small comb-footed spiders in the Theridiidae family. The Spotted Cobweaver tends to be smaller and more delicate than common house spiders, with less distinct markings than Black Widows. Its web placement in outdoor sheltered spots rather than indoor corners can help distinguish it from indoor relatives.
